Causal learning & simulation across ages: 4–5 years · 5–7 years · 7–9 years · 9–12 years · 12–25 years

Relational and analogical reasoning

During the 7-9 year window, relational and analogical reasoning undergo a qualitative reorganization. These children are undergoing the classic "relational shift": when faced with a conflict between a tempting object/scene match and a relational match (especially a higher-order relational match (e.g., the similarity between an apple falling from a tree, permitting a cow to reach it and a book falling from a shelf, permitting a child to reach it)), featural errors drop sharply across this age range as children increasingly suppress surface lures and map the higher-order relation instead (e.g., in scene analogies and A:B::C:? tasks), whereas seven-year-olds are still frequently captured by perceptual similarity (e.g similar color/shape) or, especially, semantic similarity (e.g dress-closet and milk-cow instead of dress-closet and milk-fridge 1) 2, 3, 1; this shift does, however, appear to often occur before this window but usually in a simpler, domain-specific, or language-scaffolded form 4, 3, 5. On Raven-like relational-integration tasks (similar to those seen in IQ tests), nine-year-olds outperform seven-year-olds (often by a large margin 1) and show the developmental signature of greater recruitment of prefrontal systems implicated in selecting task-relevant relations (anterior/rostrolateral PFC), further placing this age at the inflection where controlled relational retrieval and integration start to become reliable 1, 6. A 2026 study tests pattern induction across cultures (Figure) 34.

Inductive and deductive reasoning

Closely related to classification abilities, inductive reasoning (drawing generalizations from specific observations; "bottom-up") is a hallmark of Piaget’s concrete operational stage and becomes increasingly sophisticated across this window (while remaining tied to concrete observations). In line with the "relational shift", inductive reasoning shifts from featural similarity toward principled generalization with explicit attention to the informativeness of evidence: by nine, children are more likely than seven-year-olds to prefer diverse over narrow samples when projecting a property within a kind, especially when within-category variability has been highlighted 7, and they begin to treat larger samples as more reliable 8, 9, 10; before this window, it is rare to observe sensitivity to sample size and diversity 11. In naturalistic settings, 7- to 9-year-olds reliably generate inferences from repeated instances (e.g concluding "dinosaurs are big" after observing multiple big dinosaurs), detect regularities in concrete data, and use similarity and typicality (how typical an instance is compared to other category members) to induce properties and transfer them across categories 12, 13. The study also tests generalization of structured sequences (Figure).

Deductive reasoning (drawing specific conclusions from general principles; "top-down") shifts from piecemeal, premise-by-premise responding towards coordinated, model-based inference that integrates multiple premises and actively searches for counterexamples. This window sees a classic inflection point in performance on transitive inference tasks 14; seven-year-olds often treat each premise (e.g A>B) locally while nine-year-olds more reliably coordinate the ordered set (e.g., five-term A>B>C>D>E 15) and succeed on conflict items that require integrating across premises rather than recalling a single link 16, 17, 18. In conditional reasoning, nine-year-olds show a clear shift from predominantly biconditional interpretations of "if-then" statements (e.g the child assumes it rained if the street is wet) toward genuinely conditional reasoning driven by counterexample search (e.g searching for other explanations for why the ground is wet); this shift is arguably the most robust effect in the developmental conditional reasoning literature and is a signature of the logical, abstract cognition that fully emerges during ensuing developmental windows 19. Behaviorally, this appears as a rise in "uncertainty" responses on the uncertain conditional forms (e.g understanding the street being wet does not mean it certainly rained) and the first reliable spontaneous production of "disabling conditions" (counterexamples) that block modus ponens (modus ponens: "if P then Q" and "P," conclude "Q") in causal problems (e.g., "the rock hit the window but there was unbreakable film"), with both effects tightly tied to the child’s ability to retrieve alternative causes from memory 20, 21.

Counterfactual reasoning and episodic future thinking

Relative to the 7-year-old baseline, 9-year-olds’ counterfactual reasoning is notably more "causal-structure respecting": instead of solving "what if P had happened?" by simply discarding inconvenient story facts (basic conditional reasoning), they increasingly preserve the actual sequence of events and make the minimal change needed to accommodate the antecedent (the "nearest-possible-world" constraint), which is the hallmark of genuine counterfactual reasoning. Behaviorally, this shows up as near-ceiling, robust performance on singly-determined problems and a rising success rate on classic over-/doubly-determined problems that require holding an alternative cause fixed and knowing "it would still have happened because…". Performance on these problems does, however, vary broadly, in one instance between chance levels 22 and 90-100% success rates 23. One study involving a real-world, memory-scaffolded task showed that 6- to 7-year-olds could solve doubly-determined questions at a  70% success rate while 8- to 9-year-olds were near-perfect, suggesting that by 9 they can preserve the actual structure and selectively negate just the targeted cause 23 (i.e they are no longer solving via "basic conditional" shortcuts). This task was "memory-scaffolded" in comparison to an earlier design 24 where the child would have to spontaneously retrieve the second cause from memory at test, with no visual cues (e.g the full end-state of the system 25) available and even control questions steering attention back to the main actor (e.g children saw Carol and Max dirtying a clean floor, then were asked "If Carol had taken her dirty shoes off, would the floor be clean or dirty?" 22); this earlier design saw 9-year-olds falling to chance-level performance 22, suggesting that counterfactual reasoning is still not a fully-internalized or reliably-deployed cognitive function but is nonetheless becoming more principled/robust in real time. A breakthrough does, however, appear to occur during the next developmental stage (9-12 years). Counterfactual reasoning depends on a similarity ordering of worlds. (Figure). The centring of the spheres separates the two reasoning styles. (Figure).

Scientific reasoning

Following these advancements in domain-general pattern recognition and reasoning, across the 7-9-year window, children’s scientific reasoning begins to reorganize from largely outcome-driven tinkering toward more explicitly hypothesis- and evidence-guided experimentation, but remains fragile, context-sensitive, and strongly constrained by pragmatic goals. Seven- to nine-year-olds rarely deploy a genuine control-of-variables strategy (VOTAT) spontaneously: left on their own, they typically vary several factors at once, treat any successful outcome as confirming their hunch, and only reliably use unconfounded comparisons when these are modeled, heavily scaffolded, or made highly salient in the task structure 26, 27, 28. Yet when asked to design and reflect on their own investigations, most 2nd graders ( 7-8 years) and an even larger fraction of 4th-5th graders ( 9-11 years) can already conceptualize multiple "spheres" of uncertainty in an inquiry-uncertainty about how to produce the outcome, about the data themselves, about the reliability of an apparent trend, about whether it generalizes, and about which theory best explains it-and can propose concrete modifications (e.g., collecting more trials, refining measures, or changing the manipulation) to reduce the particular uncertainty they notice 29. In everyday causal scenarios that invite experimentation (e.g., why a cake failed or a paper airplane flew well), 7- to 9-year-olds flexibly choose among vary-one-thing-at-a-time (VOTAT), hold-one-thing-at-a-time (HOTAT), and change-all strategies, but their strategy selection is still governed more by a desire to preserve good outcomes and eliminate bad ones than by a norm of unconfounded testing: even by nine, they tend to hold the suspected causal factor constant when the outcome was positive and only selectively shift toward diagnostic VOTAT experiments for negative outcomes 30. In structured discovery tasks that explicitly pit plausible against implausible hypotheses (e.g., inferring what a "mystery key" does on a programmable robot), children in this age range can generate rival hypotheses but mainly use experiments to confirm the most plausible one (confirmation bias); only occasionally do they adopt the more advanced, adult-like heuristics of restricting their search to informative experiments that discriminate between alternatives and systematically attending to one feature at a time 31. Limitations aside, the capacity to generate conclusive tests of concrete hypotheses (including a search for disconfirming or falsifying evidence) is rarely found before this developmental window, reflecting intensifying abstraction of information-seeking behaviors 32, 33.

Conclusion

By around nine years of age, a child’s causal learning and simulation abilities form a genuinely generative, but still concrete-bound, world model. They can track higher-order relational structure across events, use both inductive and deductive constraints to narrow down plausible causes, and increasingly treat "if-then" claims as genuinely conditional, searching for counterexamples rather than automatically accepting a favored story. Their counterfactual simulations tend to respect the actual causal skeleton of events and make minimal changes ("it still would have happened because…"), especially when the situation is well supported by memory or external cues, and they can project the downstream consequences of alternative actions in ways that guide everyday decision-making. At the same time, their experimentation remains outcome-driven and pragmatically biased: they can talk about uncertainty, imagine informative interventions, and occasionally design near-normative tests, but their internal control-of-variables strategy is fragile, unevenly deployed, and heavily scaffolded by the task context. Overall, the nine-year-old’s causal system is best characterized as an emerging, partially explicit "intuitive scientist": capable of structured causal simulation and evidence-based revision in familiar domains, but still limited in how reliably and abstractly those skills are recruited and coordinated.
